pages.title: Pîr-i Turkistan
pages.content: Ahmed Yesevî, known as Pîr-i Turkistan, was the first great Sufi poet to write and recite his poems in plain Turkish. In the Persian language, the word ‘pîr’ means a Sufi master, spiritual guide, or elder. Yesevî was one of the most important figures in Turkish-Islamic culture. He was also the founder of the Yesevî Order (here, ‘order’ means a spiritual path). His poems are called ‘hikmet’ (wisdom). Both his poems and the Yesevî Path aimed to spread Islam among Turkish people and teach them the ways of Sufism.

pages.title: Childhood and Education
pages.content: It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram, in East Turkestan, during the second half of the 11th century. Ahmed Yesevî moved to the city of Yesi in Turkestan (which is now the city of Turkestan in Kazakhstan) at a young age. There, he studied with Arslan Baba and received a good education. He lived during the era of the Karakhanids (Karahanlılar) (840–1212) and grew up at a time when Turkestan was a center for various fields of knowledge.

pages.title: Master and Return to Yesi
pages.content:
After Arslan Baba died, Ahmed Yesevî went to Bukhara (Buhara). At that time, Bukhara was a very important center for Islam. There, Yesevî learned Islamic sciences under the guidance of Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî. He was a great scholar and a famous Sufi master who played the greatest role in training Yesevî.

When his master died, Yesevî continued his work in that area for a short time. Later, he handed over his duty as a spiritual leader to Sheikh Abdülhâlik Gucdüvânî. He then returned to Yesi and continued his spiritual guidance there until he died in 1166.

pages.title: The Yesevî Path and the Mausoleum
pages.content:
Ahmed Yesevî is still respected as a great spiritual leader by all Turkic peoples, especially the Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, and Turkmen. They call him Pîr-i Turkistan, Hoca Yesevî, or Ata Yesevî. The Yesevî Path, which he started, spread across a very large area as far as Anatolia and the Balkans. At some point between 1389 and 1405, Timur traveled to the city of Yesi and visited the tomb of Ahmed Yesevî. After that, he ordered a great building, a mausoleum, to be built over the grave. This complex also included a mosque and a center for the Sufi students. However, the construction was left unfinished when Timur died in 1405. It was very important for Central Asian Turks, the people of the steppes, to be buried near this area. For this reason, many people bought pieces of land near the mausoleum during their lives to be buried there. This tradition clearly shows the deep influence of Ahmed Yesevî.

In 2003, the historic structure was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. Its restoration, landscaping, and exterior lighting have been fully completed by TİKA (Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency). The complex is currently open to visitors, under protection, and in active use. This mausoleum and complex represent a shared cultural heritage of the Turkic-Islamic world.

A grave, often with a building over it.

pages.title: Why Turkish?
pages.content:
During Ahmed Yesevî’s time, people used Arabic for education and religion, and Persian for literature. However, Yesevî chose to write his poems in Turkish, which helped develop a Turkish identity in Islamic culture. He was a Hanafi (Hanefi) scholar who received a strict madrasa education and gained a wide knowledge of Sufism. His main goal was to spread Islam among the Turks. As a spiritual guide, he also aimed to teach the rules of Sharia (Islamic Law) and the principles of Sufism. Thanks to his followers, his Sufi path spread to many places. He sent many of the scholars he trained to Turkmen tribes to teach them the ideas of statehood and nationhood.

Ahmed Yesevî wanted to introduce Islam to Turkish communities using simple and clear teachings. He wrote about the connections between Allah, the universe, and people in a way that everyone could easily understand. He shared these ideas through simple poems, which were later collected in the book Dîvân-ı Hikmet.

pages.title: The Path of Wisdom and Society
pages.content:
According to him, the main goal of wisdom is to help people leave their ego behind and live according to the will of Allah. To achieve this, education and self-discipline are very important. People must destroy bad feelings like greed and lies, and they must develop good values like patience, love, and humility. He showed that religion is not just about sin and reward. True wisdom means being a good and real human being.

In his poems, Ahmed Yesevî did not only focus on religious topics but also wrote about social problems. In his wise words, he discussed the importance of caring for orphans and strangers, helping oppressed people, and not hurting anyone, even if they are non-believers. At the same time, he strongly criticized those who harm society, such as dishonest judges who take bribes and cruel rulers.

pages.title: Teaching with Love
pages.content:
Yesevî’s education method was centered on love. In his view, teaching students properly is only possible if you make them love what they learn. People will not accept something they do not love, even if they learn it. For this reason, teachers must treat their students with love and kindness so that students will listen to them and focus on the lessons.

The movement started by Ahmed Yesevî in Turkestan grew quickly and became very strong. Later, his teachings spread to many places and became a major Sufi path in Islamic countries, especially in the Turkic world. Through his followers, his poems even reached Turkish tribes who lived in the most distant areas. In this way, the Yesevî path spread among the Turks of Central Asia in a short time.

pages.title: The Dîvân-ı Hikmet
pages.content:
Three important works are believed to belong to Ahmed Yesevî. They reflect his Sufi ideas and teachings: the Dîvân-ı Hikmet, the Fakrnâme, and the Risale der Adab-i Tarikat. However, the texts we have today were not written by Yesevî himself. Because people passed these sayings down for generations, they were probably written down much later.

Dîvân-ı Hikmet is the title of a collection that contains Yesevî’s poems called ‘hikmet’. It is the first and most important text of Turkic Sufi literature. Hikmets are very important because they played a big role in uniting Turks around the same ideas and thoughts.

pages.title: What Is Wisdom?
pages.content:
In the Turkish-Islamic tradition, the word “wisdom” (hikmet) is very important. In fact, the Holy Qur’an is seen as a source of wisdom itself. The Qur’an looks at wisdom in two different ways. First, wisdom is a main aim of education. It helps students know the truth, understand it deeply, and make good choices. This is one of the most important goals that students are expected to achieve. Second, the Qur’an shows wisdom as a great gift from Allah and an important quality of prophets. In the end, this wisdom brings important values like honesty, justice, doing good deeds, and living with religious values.

Divine religions make rules so that people can live with faith and good morals. The ideas of “forbidden” (haram) and “permitted” (helal), and all other religious rules, are not just simple rules. The real reason behind every rule is wisdom. In Islamic law, this idea is called Makasidü’ş-şeria (the goals of Islamic law). Its purpose is to protect five important things: life, mind, religion, family, and property.

Wisdom explains the meaning and purpose of every action we take. Without wisdom, religious rules and duties are just empty tasks. While law answers the questions “What?” and “How?”, wisdom answers the question “Why?”.

Knowing what to do and how to do it is important. However, the question of ‘why’ is the most important because it gives meaning to all our actions. In the end, all rules and duties become truly important because of the wisdom behind them.

Originally, the Arabic word for wisdom means ‘to prevent.’ Wisdom protects people from ignorance and injustice. The Arabic word for ‘rule’ (hüküm) comes from the same root. Rules tell us ‘How to do’ something, but wisdom tells us ‘Why we do’ it. Without wisdom, rules have no meaning. If we do not ask ‘Why?’, religion and morals become just meaningless rules.

pages.title: Wisdom in the Qur’an and Hadith
pages.content:
Many verses in the Qur’an invite believers to look at the universe and themselves to understand the meaning of all things. Allah does not create anything without a purpose, so He does not want people to act without a purpose either. Everything we do must have a meaning and wisdom. In fact, understanding the purpose and wisdom is a very important part of every act of worship.

The Qur’an talks about wisdom in many verses. One verse states: “Allah has given you the Book and wisdom, and He has taught you what you did not know.” (Surah An-Nisa, 113) It also says, “And indeed, We gave wisdom to Luqman so that he would be thankful to Allah” (Surah Luqman, 12). In another verse, it is stated, “These are some of the wisdom that Allah gives you.” (Surah Al-Isra, 39). This means that the Qur’an cannot be understood without wisdom. The verse also states: “Allah gives wisdom to anyone He chooses. Whoever receives wisdom receives a very great blessing. However, only people with clear minds can understand this.” (Surah al-Baqarah, 269). In this sense, there is a connection between wisdom and ‘deep understanding,’ the technical term for which is ‘fiqh’ (fıkıh).

A hadith states, “Wisdom is the lost treasure of the believer; wherever he finds it, he takes it” (Ibn Mājah, “Zuhd,” 15; Tirmidhī, “ʿIlm,” 19). This defines wisdom from a broader perspective. It shows that Muslims must accept useful knowledge and true words. It does not matter who says them or where they come from.

pages.title: A Civilization of Wisdom
pages.content:
Ahmed Yesevî enlightened a very large area from Central Asia to Anatolia and the Balkans. Great thinkers who followed his path built a civilization of wisdom in Anatolia. They included Tapduk Emre, Yunus Emre, Mevlana Jalaluddin Rumi, Sadreddin Konevi, Hacı Bektaş-ı Veli, Sarı Saltuk, Baba İlyas, and Somuncu Baba. These wise people continued the Yesevî tradition. They turned cultural and geographical differences into a great and rich civilization.

Today, Ahmed Yesevî’s Dîvân-ı Hikmet is still like a spiritual home for Turkish-speaking peoples in Central Asia. They live in different countries and physical homelands now, but this book still keeps them together.

pages.title: From the Dîvân
pages.content:
Here are a few lines from his Dîvân:

“Your scholars do not like your beautiful Turkish

If you listen to the wise, they will enlighten your heart

It would be better for the verses (of the Qur’an) and the sayings of the Prophet to be in Turkish

Those who know their meanings lower their heads.”

“Sevmiyorlar bilginler sizin güzel Türkçe dilini

Bilenlerden işitsen açar gönül ilini

Âyet, hadis anlamı Türkçe olsa duyarlar

Anlamına erenler başı eğip uyarlar”

“Do not harm anybody even if he is a non-believer, which is the custom of the Prophet,

Even Allah complains about the cold-hearted and the breakers of hearts

For whom Sijjin (Hell) is ready, as Allah is the witness

I narrated these words having heard them from the wise”

“Sünnet imiş, kafir de olsa, incitme sen;

Hüdâ bîzardır (şikayetçidir, uzaktır) katı yürekli gönül incitenden.

Allah şahit, öyle kula hazırdır Siccîn (cehennem);

Bilginlerden duyup bu sözü söyledim işte.”

exercises.title: Notice: How Sure Is the Writer?
exercises.instructions: Sort the sentences: stated as fact, or presented as believed or probable?

items: In 2003, the historic structure was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
He continued his spiritual guidance there until he died in 1166.
It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram.
They were probably written down much later.

Stated as fact: In 2003, the historic structure was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
He continued his spiritual guidance there until he died in 1166.
Believed or probable: It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram.
They were probably written down much later.

exercises.explanation: Dates and recorded events are stated as facts. “It is believed that” and “probably” show that the writer is careful.
